analysis.one_liner: Rescinds new oil and gas leasing reforms and requires economic-impact certification before future federal leasing policy changes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Energy Committee without a hearing or vote, and the Interior Department's 2010 oil and gas leasing reforms stayed in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: Days after the Interior Department's Bureau of Land Management issued two memoranda adding review steps to oil and gas leasing on federal land, this bill would have wiped both memoranda out. Going forward, the Interior Secretary would have to complete an economic impact study and certify — with input from affected states — that any change to onshore oil and gas leasing policy would not cost oil and gas jobs, increase oil imports, or reduce oil and gas royalties over ten years. The bill also required public notice and comment before any leasing policy change. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be oil and gas companies leasing on federal land, which would keep the faster leasing process that existed before the May 2010 reforms and gain a new barrier — a certification of no job losses, no import increases, and no revenue losses over ten years — against any future tightening of leasing rules. Oil and gas workers in Western states and the state and county treasuries that share federal royalty revenue would gain protection as well.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal-land oil and gas producers and Western energy counties

how_it_helps.text: It rescinds two Bureau of Land Management memoranda issued May 17, 2010 that added land-use planning and lease-parcel review steps to oil and gas leasing, restoring the faster leasing process that preceded them.

It requires the Interior Secretary, before changing any onshore oil and gas leasing policy, to complete an economic impact assessment and certify that the change will not hurt oil and gas employment, increase reliance on imported petroleum, or reduce oil and gas receipts over ten years — a shield for energy jobs and royalty revenues in producing Western states.
It requires public notice and an opportunity to comment, under the Administrative Procedure Act, before any leasing policy change is implemented.

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on the public's ability to manage its own land: the Interior Department would effectively lose the power to revise oil and gas leasing policy, since almost any change could be shown to shift some jobs, imports, or receipts over a ten-year window. The rescinded memoranda had added review of lease parcels before they are offered, so removing them would mean less scrutiny of drilling on public land, with environmental and land-use costs borne by nearby communities and public-land users.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public's oversight of federal land leasing

drawbacks.text: The certification requirements would be nearly impossible to satisfy: the Secretary would have to prove, in advance and in consultation with affected states, that any leasing policy change causes no job losses, no increase in oil imports, and no loss of oil and gas receipts over ten years — a standard that would effectively freeze federal leasing policy in place and block future reforms regardless of environmental or land-use merits.

Rescinding the May 2010 BLM memoranda would strip away lease-parcel reviews and planning safeguards adopted days earlier, returning leasing to a faster process with less site-specific scrutiny before parcels of public land are offered for drilling.

The bill's economic tests treat any loss of oil and gas receipts as disqualifying, which would bar policy changes even when the lost revenue is small and the public benefit in land protection or reduced environmental damage is large.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would offer real protection to Western energy jobs, county economies, and state royalties that depend on federal leasing, and its public-comment provision adds a genuine transparency requirement. But its certification standards — proving no job loss, no import increase, and no revenue loss over ten years — are the kind of tests that are nearly impossible to certify for any policy tightening, effectively freezing the Interior Department's ability to update how public lands are leased. The public would keep the royalty revenue in the short run while losing the agency's ability to reform the program, and the rescinded memos would have imposed little cost beyond added review time. On balance, the bill's benefits flow mainly to the industry it protects, and its costs fall on the public's control of public land policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote, dying when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Bennett introduced the bill on May 19, 2010, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The full action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill was a direct response to two Bureau of Land Management leasing-reform memoranda issued May 17, 2010, which it would have rescinded and declared void.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 2010 Bureau of Land Management leasing reforms remained in place, preserving tighter review of federal oil and gas leases; the oil and gas industry did not get the certification shield it sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The 2010 leasing reforms; the industry's shield never arrived

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans — Bennett and Hatch of Utah, Barrasso and Enzi of Wyoming — and the bill never advanced far enough to draw a recorded vote from either party.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal lands
industries.note: The bill would rescind the 2010 leasing reforms that added planning and parcel reviews, and its certification requirements would make it nearly impossible for the Interior Department to tighten leasing rules in the future. Producers would get faster leases and a durable shield against policy changes. If the bill had passed, the public would bear slower environmental review of leasing decisions in exchange for the industry's lower costs.

industries.industry: State and county governments in Western energy-producing regions
industries.note: The bill protects the share of federal oil and gas royalties that flows to state treasuries by requiring certification that any policy change causes no ten-year loss of receipts. For energy-dependent counties this revenue supports schools and roads, but the protection comes at the price of locking in the leasing policies of January 2010.
